requirements.requirement: node1 has a routed address on each of its two segments (eth1 toward node2's segment, eth2 toward node3's segment)
requirements.summary: node1 eth1 shows 192.168.1.1/24 and eth2 shows 192.168.2.1/24, confirmed both pre-restart and post-restart.

requirements.requirement: working path between node2 and node3 (routed through node1)
requirements.summary: Bidirectional ping between node2 (192.168.1.2) and node3 (192.168.2.2) succeeded with 0% loss after final static/NetworkManager configuration.

requirements.requirement: configuration returns automatically after node1 restart, with node2/node3 reaching each other again once it comes back up
requirements.summary: Full bounded disruption cycle observed: pre-restart healthy baseline (boot_id 82b18f3b..., node2/node3 ping success), reboot acknowledgement and disconnection (COLD shutdown log, connection reset), post-restart boot_id changed to 70971868..., node1 eth1/eth2 addresses and forwarding sysctls restored without manual intervention, and node2<->node3 ping recovered with 0% loss after node1 came back up. The after_executor lifecycle snapshot independently corroborates the changed boot_id for node1.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task are satisfied with direct evidence: node1 has routed addresses on both segments, a working ping path exists between node2 and node3 through node1, and this configuration (including node1's addresses, forwarding, and connectivity) was shown to return automatically after a real node1 reboot (boot_id changed from 82b18f3b... to 70971868...) without manual reconfiguration. The lifecycle snapshot's boot-identity cross-check for node1 corroborates the reboot claim. Operational hygiene is good: exploratory manual networking commands during discovery were superseded or reverted, and temporary service stops on node1 were restored before task completion.
limitations: Some early command_ids returned non-zero exit codes (e.g., duplicate address/dev errors) during iterative discovery; these were not evidence of final failure since later commands confirmed the correct end state.
Node2 and node3 were not themselves restarted/rebooted in this trace, so only node1's restart-recovery behavior was directly observed; the task only required this for node1.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor performed a bounded troubleshooting sequence before reaching the persisted solution. cmd-5e42055e5de74494 temporarily flushed eth1/eth2, brought docker0 down/deleted its address, and stopped interfaces-config.service and networking.service on node1 to prevent them from reverting manual changes; these services were explicitly restarted later (cmd-dd5e5909d0064144) and docker0's address was independently regenerated by the SONiC boot process after the reboot (confirmed present again in cmd-8bda6dd0ad9e4929), so no residue remained. Several early manual ip addr add/ip route replace attempts on node1/node2/node3 (cmd-65977e1fbdad4f15, cmd-9f96594beedc4774, cmd-76ab3363ccb249ae, cmd-c2e069038c324b71, cmd-1015ee646c704421, cmd-5353de5cacb34100, cmd-3cd31afd96074607) were superseded by the final persisted configuration (SONiC interfaces.d drop-in + sysctl.d on node1, nmcli static profiles on node2/node3) and left no conflicting state, since the final verified addressing matches the persisted config exactly. No failed services, damaged package state, or unsafe exposure were introduced by the executor; the two failed systemd units present in both before_prepare and after_executor snapshots are pre-existing and unrelated to executor actions.
